photonics-electronics.name: Integrated photonics and electronics
photonics-electronics.introduction: Electronics computes; light carries information. What happens when their strengths meet?
photonics-electronics.summary: Integrating photonics and electronics brings optical technology together with electronic circuits. Electronics is well suited to computation and control, while light can carry large amounts of information. Bringing them closer aims to improve the speed and energy efficiency of communication within information systems.

sections.title: Why use light?
sections.body: Data centers do more than compute: they move enormous amounts of data between devices and chips. High-speed electrical connections face challenges including transmission losses and heat. Bringing optical communication inside devices is one approach to these problems.

sections.title: Passing information between light and electronics
sections.body: For example, a signal produced by an electronic circuit can be converted into light, sent through an optical fiber, and converted back into an electrical signal at the receiver. Research and development aim to place the components that perform these conversions close to electronic circuits, or integrate them together.

sections.title: Not every calculation becomes optical
sections.body: Integrating photonics and electronics does not mean replacing all computation with light. Conversion also requires energy and components. Deciding where to transmit information optically and where to process it electronically is an essential part of the design.

ethnography.name: Ethnography
ethnography.introduction: Look beyond what people do to understand what feels ordinary to them.
ethnography.summary: Ethnography involves engaging with people's lives and activities, using observation and dialogue to understand and describe actions and meanings in context. It developed in cultural anthropology and is now also used in fields such as organizational and design research.

sections.title: Entering everyday life
sections.body: Questionnaire answers alone may not reveal everyday behavior or unspoken rules. Researchers spend time in the field, combining participant observation—observing while taking part in activities—with interviews and the examination of records and other materials.

sections.title: What a cup of tea can reveal
sections.body: Consider a workplace tea break. What looks like a simple pause may also be a chance to discuss work or offer advice to a newcomer. This is a fictional illustration: it shows how ethnography asks what an action means in its setting, rather than only counting how often it happens.

sections.title: Questioning the observer's perspective
sections.body: An observation does not automatically become the only truth. An account depends on whom the researcher engaged with and how they interpreted events. Consent, privacy, and reflection on the researcher's own position are essential.

surrealism.name: Surrealism
surrealism.introduction: Let the strangeness of dreams unsettle familiar reality.
surrealism.summary: Surrealism is an artistic and literary movement that explored dreams and the unconscious, seeking expression beyond the limits of reason and convention. André Breton's 1924 Surrealist Manifesto was an important milestone.

sections.title: More than strange paintings
sections.body: Surrealism is known for paintings that combine things in seemingly impossible ways, but it also spread into poetry, writing, photography, and film. Beyond novelty, it questioned ways of seeing reality that are usually taken for granted.

sections.title: Writing before conscious editing
sections.body: One practice was automatic writing: letting words emerge while holding back the impulse to organize them logically or polish the language. It reflected an interest in the unconscious, but the resulting writing should not be treated as a scientific measurement of the mind.

sections.title: New encounters between familiar things
sections.body: An everyday object can take on a different meaning when it appears somewhere unexpected. Surrealism used such encounters and displacements to explore possibilities beyond ordinary arrangements. Methods varied across works and artists.

optical-fiber.name: Optical fiber
optical-fiber.introduction: A thin strand guides light to carry information.
optical-fiber.summary: In optical communication, a fiber that guides light serves as a transmission medium. It is not synonymous with integrating photonics and electronics; it is one technology that supports the transmission of information using light.

ccd.name: CCD
ccd.introduction: A semiconductor circuit that captures light electronically for imaging.
ccd.summary: A CCD records light as electronic signals. It helped make it possible to record photographs electronically rather than only on film. Not every digital camera uses a CCD.

photography.name: Photography
photography.introduction: A way to record light, and a medium for expression.
photography.summary: Photography records light to form images. Here, electronic recording using CCDs and Man Ray's photographic works introduced by MoMA offer two starting points for exploring its technological and artistic aspects.

dada.name: Dada
dada.introduction: Questioning established art through chance, everyday objects, and unexpected materials.
dada.summary: Dada was an artistic and literary movement that emerged during the First World War. Its practitioners used diverse materials and methods, including collage, photomontage, and everyday objects.

collage.name: Collage
collage.introduction: Bringing different fragments together into one work.
collage.summary: Collage combines fragments of material, such as pieces of paper. MoMA presents Hans Arp's chance-based collages among the practices associated with Dada.

user-research.name: User research
user-research.introduction: Studying people's behavior and circumstances to inform design decisions.
user-research.summary: One approach visits people in their usual environments and observes their activities. Tools and surroundings help reveal what a service needs to support. User research is not equivalent to ethnography as a whole.

user-centered-design.name: User-centered design
user-centered-design.introduction: Design begins with understanding people's goals and circumstances.
user-centered-design.summary: The GOV.UK Service Standard calls for understanding users and their problems, then testing assumptions through research and prototypes. It starts with what people need to achieve, rather than choosing a solution in advance.

optical-communication.name: Optical communication
optical-communication.summary: Technology that transmits information using light, including communication through optical fiber.

silicon-photonics.name: Silicon photonics
silicon-photonics.summary: Technology for building small optical circuits and components on a silicon platform.

participant-observation.name: Participant observation
participant-observation.summary: A research method that combines taking part in people's activities with observation to understand practices and meanings in context.

fieldnotes.name: Fieldnotes
fieldnotes.summary: Notes recording events and conversations in the field, alongside the researcher's observations and interpretations.

automatism.name: Automatic writing
automatism.summary: An expressive method of recording words as they arise while holding back conscious editing.

andre-breton.name: André Breton
andre-breton.summary: A French poet and writer who was one of the leading figures of the Surrealist movement.

light.name: Light
light.summary: Light is used both to transmit information and to record images. This does not mean the two uses have the same purpose.

ethnography-photography.label: One way to document research
ethnography-photography.explanation: Ethnographic practices can use photographs to record and interpret lives and activities. Photographs carry context and the photographer's perspective; photography alone does not replace the whole research process.

surrealism-photography.label: An expressive medium
surrealism-photography.explanation: Surrealism included photographic practices such as photomontage and photograms. Their aims differ from photography used in research. This connection does not claim a direct historical influence between Surrealism and anthropology.

photonics-communication.label: A technology it uses
photonics-communication.explanation: Integrating photonics and electronics combines electronic circuits with optical information transmission. Optical communication supports the transfer of information between and within devices.

photonics-silicon.label: One enabling technology
photonics-silicon.explanation: Silicon photonics integrates optical components at a small scale and is one way to bring light and electronic circuits closer. It does not describe the whole field of integrating photonics and electronics.

ethnography-observation.label: A major research method
ethnography-observation.explanation: Ethnography uses participant observation to understand the context of people's lives and activities. Interviews and examination of documents and other materials are also used.

ethnography-notes.label: A way to record research
ethnography-notes.explanation: Fieldnotes record observed events, conversations, and the researcher's interpretations. Revisiting these records supports description and analysis.

surrealism-automatism.label: An expressive method
surrealism-automatism.explanation: Surrealism explored dreams and the unconscious and practiced automatic writing as one form of expression. This method alone does not explain the entire movement.

breton-surrealism.label: One of the movement's leaders
breton-surrealism.explanation: Breton published the Surrealist Manifesto in 1924 and helped lead the movement, which involved many writers and artists.

photonics-electronics--light.label: Used to transmit information
photonics-electronics--light.explanation: Integrating photonics and electronics combines optical input and output with electronic circuits.

optical-fiber--optical-communication.label: Provides a transmission medium
optical-fiber--optical-communication.explanation: Optical fiber guides light as a transmission medium in optical communication.

ccd--light.label: Detects light for recording
ccd--light.explanation: A CCD is a semiconductor imaging circuit that captures light electronically.

photography--light.label: Records it as an image
photography--light.explanation: Electronic photography uses imaging sensors such as CCDs to capture light.

photography--ccd.label: One electronic recording method
photography--ccd.explanation: CCDs are one technology used to record photographs electronically.

dada--collage.label: One expressive method
dada--collage.explanation: MoMA presents collage among Dada's methods, including Hans Arp's chance-based work.

dada--photography.label: Uses photographic fragments too
dada--photography.explanation: Dada includes photomontage, which combines fragments of photographs.

user-research--participant-observation.label: Uses observation in context
user-research--participant-observation.explanation: User research can also observe activities in everyday settings. The degree of participation varies across studies; the two methods are not identical.

user-research--fieldnotes.label: Records observations in context
user-research--fieldnotes.explanation: GOV.UK's contextual research guidance describes recording what is seen and heard in notes. Recording also supports analysis in ethnography.

user-centered-design--user-research.label: Deepens understanding of users
user-centered-design--user-research.explanation: The GOV.UK Service Standard calls for user research to understand what people need when designing a service.
